<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but A's core mechanism—that cash literally cannot summon supply where markets have failed (childcare/transit deserts) or cover catastrophic costs (cancer treatment)—proved harder for B to neutralize than B's heterogeneity/rigidity argument was for A. The decisive exchange came in the Pressure Questions and Rebuttal 2: when pressed on catastrophic illness, B's answer ("insurance") and on deserts ("informal care, co-ops, ride-shares") both quietly abandoned the "unconditional cash" premise the motion actually specifies, substituting earmarked or informal workarounds. A explicitly caught this ("insurance is money that is earmarked... you cannot use a premium to fix your roof"), turning B's own answers into concessions that pure cash fails exactly where stakes are highest. B's counter-pressure question (why government-run rather than subsidized insurance) was sharp and exposed a real gap in A's case about direct provision versus funding, but A's closing reframed the pattern effectively ("every time CON faces a concrete need, they answer with something other than the check"), which was never fully rebutted. B's closing reasserted that this was a narrow retreat, but did not resolve the underlying inconsistency of invoking non-cash mechanisms while defending "unconditional cash transfers." That unresolved tension gives A the cleaner, more damaging rebuttal thread across the debate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1), turning B's "subsidized insurance" answer into an admission that earmarked/pooled spending—A's own principle—is required to solve catastrophic risk, which B never fully disentangled from the motion's cash-vs-services framing.</best_rebuttal>
